body:
Most of the legends share a common core. They want a business they understand, one that earns high and durable returns on capital (a "moat"), run by honest owner-minded management, and bought at a price below a conservative estimate of intrinsic value. They then hold it for a long time. The investors differ mainly in where they look:
- Graham looks at cheap assets and earnings.
- Fisher, Lynch and Mayer look at growth.
- Sleep looks at scale economics that the company shares with customers.
- Pabrai looks at asymmetric bets.
- Smith looks at high ROCE combined with "do nothing".

`case_study:kingfisher-ub-2012` | 2012-10-20 | tickers: UBHOLDINGS | confidence: verified

Kingfisher Airlines launched in 2005 and never posted an annual profit. It bought low-cost Air Deccan in 2007 at a premium, mixing a full-service and a low-cost model. By Mar 2013 accumulated losses were ~Rs 16,023 cr and net worth ~-Rs 12,920 cr. DGCA suspended its licence in Oct 2012; dues to a 17-bank SBI-led consortium were ~Rs 9,000 cr+. Vijay Mallya left India in Mar 2016 and has disputed fraud charges. Visible flags: (1) losses every year plus negative net worth; (2) 2010-11 debt restructuring where banks converted loans to equity at a large premium (~Rs 64.48/share) to market -- lenders throwing good money after bad; (3) the Kingfisher brand was used as collateral at a ~Rs 4,000 cr valuation -- intangible collateral; (4) personal and corporate guarantees across UB Holdings, cross-holdings with United Spirits/United Breweries; (5) salary and tax-deduction (TDS/PF) defaults in 2011-12; (6) promoter pledges in group companies (later United Spirits went to Diageo in 2012-13). Lesson: a premium 'lifestyle' brand cannot rescue an airline with negative equity; when lenders accept brand value as security or convert debt at a premium, equity holders are next in line for losses. Cross-guarantees mean one group company can drag others.

**Lesson:** Intangible collateral + negative equity = terminal
**Spotted early by:** staff (unpaid salaries), aviation analysts
**Links:** illustrates -> `insight:disqualifiers`, illustrates -> `insight:promoter-pledge-group-contagion`

`person:group-religare-singh` · flag: **severe** · confidence: verified · tickers: FORTIS, RELIGARE

Flag: SEVERE (Singh era); Fortis (IHH-controlled since 2018) and Religare (Burman-controlled since 2025) have new promoters. The Singh brothers sold Ranbaxy to Daiichi Sankyo (2008, ~$4.6bn); Daiichi later won a ~Rs 3,500 cr Singapore arbitration award (2016) for concealment of US FDA issues. They then extracted value from Fortis Healthcare and Religare: Fortis disclosed ~Rs 473-500 cr of inter-corporate deposits routed to promoter-linked entities (2017-18), auditor Deloitte qualified results, and the board was overhauled; RBI (2018) found Religare Finvest (RFL) had placed ~Rs 2,300 cr+ of corporate loans with promoter-linked shells; Delhi Police EOW arrested both brothers (Oct-2019) in the ~Rs 2,397 cr RFL misappropriation case; ED followed under PMLA. The Supreme Court held the brothers guilty of contempt (Nov-2019) for selling Fortis shares in violation of its order and sentenced them to six months (Sep-2022). The Delhi HC granted Malvinder bail in the EOW case (2023); a Delhi court framed conspiracy/cheating charges; Shivinder filed for personal insolvency (2025). No final criminal verdict found as of 2026. Early signals: promoter pledges near 100% at Fortis/Religare, ICDs to promoter entities, auditor qualifications, spiritual-guru (RSSB) related borrowings reported, and an unexplained cash gap after selling Ranbaxy.

- **regulator findings:** RBI 2018 RFL inspection; SC contempt (2019, sentence 2022)

`insight:buffett-2000-bubble-ipo-wealth-transfer` | confidence: verified | date: 2001-02-28

2000 letter (written early 2001, after the dot-com peak): 'value is destroyed, not created, by any business that loses money over its lifetime, no matter how high its interim valuation may get.' What happens instead is 'wealth transfer, often on a massive scale. By shamelessly merchandising birdless bushes, promoters have in recent years moved billions of dollars from the pockets of the public to their own purses'; 'a bubble market has allowed the creation of bubble companies, entities designed more with an eye to making money off investors rather than for them. Too often, an IPO, not profits, was the primary goal of a company's promoters.' The 'business model' was 'the old-fashioned chain letter, for which many fee-hungry investment bankers acted as eager postmen.' 'But a pin lies in wait for every bubble.' On psychology: 'Nothing sedates rationality like large doses of effortless money'; speculators plan to leave the ball 'just seconds before midnight. There's a problem, though: They are dancing in a room in which the clocks have no hands.' Evidence he cites: a Dec-1999 PaineWebber-Gallup survey where investors expected ~19% annual returns for the next decade. Actionable for India: SME/mainboard IPO frenzies (record subscriptions, grey-market premia, OFS-heavy issues where promoters/PE sell) are the modern version; check whether proceeds go to the company or to selling holders.

Sources:
- https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/2000pdf.pdf
